title: Social Roles (Stanford Prison Experiment)
description: When placed in a role with defined power and rules, people quickly adopt behaviors and attitudes consistent with that role—often to extremes they would never have predicted. The situation can override personality.
shortDescription: When placed in a role with defined power and rules, people quickly adopt behaviors and attitudes consistent with that role—often to extremes they would never have predicted. The situation can override personality.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: When placed in a role with defined power and rules, people quickly adopt behaviors and attitudes consistent with that role—often to extremes they would never have predicted. The situation can override personality.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A new manager, previously a supportive colleague, suddenly becomes authoritarian because “that’s what a manager should be.”
In a police force, good officers can become abusive because the role and uniform grant them power and the environment normalizes it.
A quiet student becomes a loud, assertive leader when assigned a team captain role.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Adopting the language and posture associated with the role.
De‑personalizing others based on their role (e.g., seeing prisoners as “subjects,” employees as “resources”).
Feeling that “I was just playing the role” but the role becomes the person.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “I’m not like this normally, but I had to be the boss.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You notice your personality shifting to fit a title or uniform.
You begin to view people through the lens of their role, not their humanity.
The situation makes cruelty feel “normal” and kindness feel out of place.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Philip Zimbardo’s Stanford Prison Experiment (1971), despite its ethical and methodological criticisms, illustrated a real tendency: people conform powerfully to assigned roles, especially when those roles have clearly defined power differences and when the environment supports them. The effect has been observed in real prisons, corporate hierarchies, and schools.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Define the role, don’t let the role define you. Regularly ask: “Am I being this way because it’s me, or because of the title?”
Rotate roles or limit power concentration.
Maintain contact with people who knew you before the role and can call out changes.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming only weak people fall into role conformity. Studies show most people adapt rapidly, often without realizing.
Believing you can “handle it” without safeguards. Power’s influence is gradual and self‑justifying.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A newly promoted team lead, who used to be the most empathetic colleague, starts micromanaging and belittling his former peers. Within months, he’s alienated everyone and can’t see why. He says, “It’s my job to keep them in line.” The role consumed his personality.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Roles are scripts. If you don’t write your own, the situation will write it for you—and it may turn you into a character you never wanted to play.
